questions.text: Which component is known as the brain of the computer?
questions.explanation: CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the primary component that executes instructions and processes data.

questions.text: What does DNS stan d for?
questions.explanation: DNS stands for Domain Name System - it translates domain names like google.com into IP addresses.

questions.text: Which of the following is a programming language?
questions.explanation: C++ is a general-purpose programming language. HTML, HTTP and JSON are markup/protocol/data formats.

questions.text: What does OOP stand for?
questions.explanation: OOP stands for Object Oriented Programming - a paradigm based on objects and classes.

questions.text: What is a variable?
options: A named storage location in memory
questions.explanation: A variable is a named storage location in memory that holds a value which can change during execution.

questions.text: What does int stand for in C++?
questions.explanation: int stands for Integer - a data type that stores whole numbers.

questions.text: What is RAM?
questions.explanation: RAM stands for Random Access Memory - temporary storage that the CPU uses to store data currently in use.

questions.text: What is a GPU primarily used for?
questions.explanation: GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) was originally designed for rendering graphics but is now also used for parallel computing tasks.

questions.text: What does SSD stand for?
questions.explanation: SSD stands for Solid State Drive - a storage device that uses flash memory instead of spinning disks.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a motherboard?
options: To connect all components of a computer
questions.explanation: The motherboard is the main circuit board that connects and allows communication between all components of a computer.

questions.text: What does HTTP stand for?
questions.explanation: HTTP stands for HyperText Transfer Protocol - the foundation of data communication on the World Wide Web.

questions.text: What is an IP address?
options: A unique numerical identifier for a device on a network
questions.explanation: An IP address is a unique numerical label assigned to each device connected to a network.

questions.text: What does VPN stand for?
questions.explanation: VPN stands for Virtual Private Network - it creates an encrypted connection over a public network.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a firewall?
options: To monitor and control incoming and outgoing network traffic
questions.explanation: A firewall monitors and controls network traffic based on security rules to protect a network from unauthorized access.

questions.text: What is the kernel of an operating system?
options: The core component that manages hardware and system resources
questions.explanation: The kernel is the core of an OS that manages communication between hardware and software.

questions.text: What does CLI stand for?
questions.explanation: CLI stands for Command Line Interface - a text-based interface for interacting with a computer.

questions.text: What is a process in an operating system?
questions.explanation: A process is an instance of a program that is being executed by the operating system.

questions.text: What does GUI stand for?
questions.explanation: GUI stands for Graphical User Interface - a visual interface that allows users to interact with a computer using graphics.

questions.text: What is a file system?
options: A method for organizing and storing files on a storage device
questions.explanation: A file system is a method used by operating systems to organize, store, and retrieve data on storage devices.

questions.text: What is a pointer in C++?
options: A variable that stores a memory address
A function that returns a value
questions.explanation: A pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable.

questions.text: What does TCP stand for?
questions.explanation: TCP stands for Transmission Control Protocol - it ensures reliable, ordered delivery of data between applications.

questions.text: What is the difference between HDD and SSD?
options: HDD uses flash memory, SSD uses spinning disks
SSD uses flash memory, HDD uses spinning disks
questions.explanation: SSD uses flash memory with no moving parts, while HDD uses spinning magnetic disks. SSDs are faster but traditionally more expensive.

questions.text: What is a subnet mask?
options: A number that defines the network and host portions of an IP address
questions.explanation: A subnet mask is a 32-bit number that divides an IP address into network and host portions.

questions.text: What is inheritance in OOP?
options: A mechanism where a class acquires properties of another class
questions.explanation: Inheritance is an OOP mechanism that allows a class to inherit properties and methods from another class.

questions.text: What is virtual memory?
options: A technique that uses disk space to extend RAM
questions.explanation: Virtual memory is a technique that allows the OS to use disk space as an extension of RAM when physical memory is full.

questions.text: What is a MAC address?
options: An address used only on Apple devices
A unique hardware identifier assigned to a network interface
questions.explanation: A MAC address is a unique hardware identifier assigned to a network interface card by the manufacturer.

questions.text: What is the clock speed of a CPU measured in?
questions.explanation: CPU clock speed is measured in GHz (Gigahertz) and represents how many cycles per second the processor can execute.

questions.text: What is a constructor in OOP?
options: A special method called when an object is created
questions.explanation: A constructor is a special method that is automatically called when an object of a class is instantiated.

questions.text: What does BIOS stand for?
questions.explanation: BIOS stands for Basic Input Output System - firmware that initializes hardware during the boot process.

questions.text: What is multithreading in an OS?
options: Running multiple threads of a process simultaneously
questions.explanation: Multithreading allows a single process to run multiple threads simultaneously, improving performance on multi-core processors.

questions.text: What is the purpose of ARP in networking?
options: To map IP addresses to MAC addresses
questions.explanation: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on a local network.

questions.text: What is a stack in programming?
questions.explanation: A stack is a LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) data structure where the last element added is the first to be removed.

questions.text: What does DHCP stand for?
questions.explanation: DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses and other network configuration to devices on a network.

questions.text: What is cache memory?
options: Small high-speed memory located close to the CPU
questions.explanation: Cache memory is small, fast memory located close to the CPU that stores frequently accessed data.

questions.text: What is a deadlock in an operating system?
options: A situation where two or more processes are stuck waiting for each other
questions.explanation: A deadlock occurs when two or more processes are each waiting for the other to release a resource, causing all of them to be stuck.

questions.text: What is encapsulation in OOP?
options: Wrapping data in a capsule shape
Bundling data and methods that operate on that data within a class
questions.explanation: Encapsulation bundles data and the methods that operate on it within a class, hiding internal details from outside.

questions.text: What is NAT in networking?
questions.explanation: NAT translates private IP addresses to a public IP address, allowing multiple devices to share one public IP.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a CPU cooler?
options: To prevent the CPU from overheating
questions.explanation: A CPU cooler dissipates heat generated by the processor to prevent overheating and thermal throttling.

questions.text: What is a semaphore in an OS?
options: A synchronization tool used to control access to shared resources
questions.explanation: A semaphore is a synchronization mechanism used to control access to shared resources in concurrent programming.

questions.text: What is polymorphism in OOP?
options: The ability of objects to take many forms
questions.explanation: Polymorphism allows objects of different classes to be treated as objects of a common superclass, with each responding differently to the same method call.

questions.text: What is the OSI model?
options: A conceptual framework with 7 layers describing network communication
questions.explanation: The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model is a 7-layer framework that standardizes network communication functions.

questions.text: What is pipelining in a CPU?
options: A technique where multiple instructions are overlapped in execution
questions.explanation: Pipelining allows a CPU to overlap the execution of multiple instructions, improving throughput.

questions.text: What is a race condition in OS?
options: A situation where the output depends on the sequence of uncontrollable events
questions.explanation: A race condition occurs when multiple processes access shared data simultaneously and the outcome depends on execution order.

questions.text: What is a lambda function?
options: A Greek letter used in math
questions.explanation: A lambda function is an anonymous function that can be defined inline without a name, useful for short operations.

questions.text: What is HTTPS?
options: HTTP with SSL/TLS encryption for secure communication
questions.explanation: HTTPS is HTTP with SSL/TLS encryption, providing secure communication between a browser and web server.

questions.text: What is overclocking?
options: Setting the wrong time on a computer
Running a CPU or GPU faster than its rated speed
questions.explanation: Overclocking is the practice of running a CPU or GPU at a higher clock speed than officially specified to gain performance.

questions.text: What is a page fault in an OS?
options: An error in a web browser
When a program accesses a memory page not currently in RAM
questions.explanation: A page fault occurs when a program tries to access a memory page that is not currently loaded in RAM, causing the OS to load it from disk.

questions.text: What is a template in C++?
options: A feature that allows writing generic code that works with any data type
questions.explanation: Templates in C++ allow writing generic functions and classes that work with any data type.

questions.text: What is BGP in networking?
options: Border Gateway Protocol used to route traffic between autonomous systems
questions.explanation: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the routing protocol used to exchange routing information between autonomous systems on the internet.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a PSU in a computer?
options: To convert AC power to DC power for computer components
questions.explanation: A PSU (Power Supply Unit) converts AC power from the wall outlet to DC power used by computer components.

questions.text: What is context switching in an OS?
options: Saving and restoring the state of a process so the CPU can switch between processes
questions.explanation: Context switching is the process of saving the state of a running process and loading the state of another, allowing the CPU to multitask.

questions.text: What is the difference between a class and an object?
options: A class is a blueprint, an object is an instance of that blueprint
An object is a blueprint, a class is an instance
questions.explanation: A class is a blueprint or template that defines attributes and methods, while an object is a specific instance created from that class.

questions.text: What is SSL/TLS?
options: Cryptographic protocols that provide secure communication over a network
questions.explanation: SSL/TLS are cryptographic protocols that encrypt data transmitted over networks, ensuring security and privacy.

questions.text: What is thermal throttling?
options: When a CPU reduces its speed to prevent overheating
questions.explanation: Thermal throttling occurs when a CPU or GPU automatically reduces its clock speed to prevent damage from excessive heat.

questions.text: What is a mutex?
options: A synchronization primitive that prevents multiple threads from accessing a resource simultaneously
questions.explanation: A mutex (mutual exclusion) is a locking mechanism that ensures only one thread can access a shared resource at a time.

questions.text: What is the difference between stack and heap memory?
options: Stack is automatic/fast for local variables, heap is dynamic/manual for allocated memory
Stack is only used in Python
questions.explanation: Stack memory is automatically managed and used for local variables, while heap memory is manually allocated and used for dynamic data.

questions.text: What is a VLAN?
options: A logical network segment that groups devices regardless of physical location
questions.explanation: A VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) logically segments a network, grouping devices together regardless of their physical location.

questions.text: How many cores does a dual-core processor have?
questions.explanation: A dual-core processor has 2 cores, allowing it to process two tasks simultaneously.

questions.text: What is scheduling in an OS?
options: Determining the order in which processes get CPU time
questions.explanation: CPU scheduling determines the order in which processes in the ready queue get access to the CPU.

questions.text: What is an abstract class?
options: A class that cannot be instantiated and must be subclassed
questions.explanation: An abstract class cannot be instantiated directly and serves as a blueprint for other classes that must implement its abstract methods.

questions.text: What is latency in networking?
options: The time delay for data to travel from source to destination
questions.explanation: Latency is the time it takes for data to travel from its source to its destination, typically measured in milliseconds.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a heat sink?
options: To absorb and dissipate heat from components like the CPU
questions.explanation: A heat sink absorbs heat from components like the CPU and dissipates it into the surrounding air.

questions.text: What is the difference between 32-bit and 64-bit OS?
options: 64-bit can address more memory and process larger data chunks
questions.explanation: A 64-bit OS can address vastly more memory (theoretically 16 exabytes) and process larger data chunks than a 32-bit OS which is limited to 4GB RAM.

questions.text: What is a linked list?
options: A data structure where each element points to the next
questions.explanation: A linked list is a data structure where each element (node) contains data and a pointer to the next node.

questions.text: What is bandwidth in networking?
options: The width of a network cable
The maximum data transfer rate of a network
questions.explanation: Bandwidth is the maximum amount of data that can be transmitted over a network in a given time, measured in bits per second.

questions.text: What is PCIe?
options: Peripheral Component Interconnect Express - a high-speed interface for connecting components
questions.explanation: PCIe (Peripheral Component Interconnect Express) is a high-speed serial interface used to connect graphics cards, SSDs, and other components.

questions.text: What is a zombie process?
options: A process that has finished but its entry remains in the process table
questions.explanation: A zombie process has completed execution but still has an entry in the process table because its parent hasn't read its exit status.

questions.text: What is a destructor in C++?
options: A special method called when an object is destroyed to free resources
questions.explanation: A destructor is a special method automatically called when an object goes out of scope or is deleted, used to free allocated resources.

questions.text: What is a load balancer?
options: A device that distributes network traffic across multiple servers
questions.explanation: A load balancer distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers to ensure no single server becomes overwhelmed.

questions.text: What does DDR stand for in DDR RAM?
questions.explanation: DDR stands for Double Data Rate - it transfers data on both the rising and falling edges of the clock cycle, doubling throughput.

questions.text: What is I/O scheduling in an OS?
options: Managing and ordering requests to I/O devices to optimize performance
questions.explanation: I/O scheduling orders and manages requests to input/output devices like hard drives to minimize seek time and maximize throughput.

questions.text: What is the difference between == and = in C++?
questions.explanation: In C++, = is the assignment operator that stores a value, while == is the equality comparison operator that checks if two values are equal.

questions.text: What is CDN in networking?
options: Content Delivery Network - servers distributed geographically to deliver content faster
questions.explanation: A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a system of distributed servers that deliver web content to users based on their geographic location.

questions.text: What is the purpose of thermal paste?
options: To glue the CPU to the motherboard
To improve heat transfer between the CPU and heat sink
questions.explanation: Thermal paste fills microscopic gaps between the CPU and heat sink, improving thermal conductivity and heat transfer.

questions.text: What is memory fragmentation in an OS?
options: Inefficient use of memory where free space is broken into small unusable chunks
questions.explanation: Memory fragmentation occurs when free memory is divided into small, non-contiguous chunks, making it difficult to allocate large blocks.

questions.text: What is a pure virtual function in C++?
options: A virtual function with no implementation that must be overridden in derived classes
questions.explanation: A pure virtual function is declared with = 0 and has no implementation in the base class, forcing derived classes to provide their own implementation.
